text: {"headline":"Provider 1000000200 bills 99215 well above expectation, including heavily on low-complexity patients, but every documented 99215 chart supports the billed level, and note-quality signals raise questions about whether that documentation reflects the actual visits.","leaning":"inconclusive","interpretation":"The excess 99215 rate holds in every complexity stratum. The sampled low-complexity 99215 claims are the concern: they include single acute problems on patients with no chronic conditions, such as an upper respiratory infection (C0117131) and a urinary tract infection in an 18-year-old (C0117500). Against that, all 17 documented 99215 claims were supported at the billed level, with examples like C0117000 and C0117175 showing high MDM. Taken alone, that would point toward a legitimately complex panel. The documentation is a thin sample of about 6% of claims with no audit trail, and the notes show warning signs: about a third flagged as duplicate, problems and late flags, and data-reviewed claims without matching lab or test lines (e.g., C0117019). These are weak signs of cloned or inflated notes, not proof. A reviewer should first pull charts for the sampled low-complexity 99215 claims and compare their note text for duplication, then request the EHR audit trail to see when and how the notes were created."}
